L5: //
L6: // Stage one resets the terminal and prints the card, then replaces itself with
L7: // stage two, which waits for a key. Printing expands the card in the shell's
L8: // memory, and a shell that kept that copy would hold it for as long as the
L9: // window naps; a new process image holds nothing but its own arguments.
L10: //
L11: // The first byte is read by `dd`: dash has no single-byte `read`, and bash's
L12: // `read -n 1` switches the terminal back to signal mode, so Ctrl-C would kill
L13: // the stub instead of waking it. The rest of an escape or mouse sequence is
L14: // drained by the `read` builtin until 0.1 s passes with no input.
L15: //
L16: // With <wake> set to `focus`, the terminal also reports focus. Focus in wakes
L17: // the window like a key; focus out (`ESC [ O`, whose first byte `dd` took)
L18: // goes back to waiting.
L19: //
L20: // A plain `opencode` first checks the background service, and replaces it
L21: // when it does not answer in time, which ends every window's shells. Windows
L22: // that wake together keep a busy service busy, so a wake that finds the
L23: // service registered and running connects to it with --server instead, which
L24: // never replaces it. `field` reads the registration, written by
L25: // JSON.stringify on one line, with shell patterns: no parser is needed, and a
L26: // value with an escape in it is refused rather than guessed at. The version
L27: // must be the one the window napped from, so a registration left by another
L28: // channel or release is not taken for this window's service.
L29: //
L30: // While the service is busy, curl waits for it, so the TUI's own short check
L31: // succeeds; its password reaches curl on stdin (`-q` keeps ~/.curlrc out of
L32: // it) and OpenCode in the environment, never in an argument. The wait has no
L33: // limit, because giving up would be the restart this avoids; Ctrl-C ends it
L34: // and starts the usual way. A registration that is missing, stale, for
L35: // another version, or a service that refuses, has failed or is not
L36: // listening, falls back to the plain start, which starts or repairs the
L37: // service as before.

# opencode-nap [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/opencode-nap?logo=npm&style=flat-square)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/opencode-nap) [![License](https://img.shields.io/npm/l/opencode-nap?style=flat-square)](./LICENSE) An OpenCode 2 plugin that puts idle terminal windows to sleep to free memory, and wakes them into the same session when you come back: refocus the window, or press a key or click. ![Ten idle windows: 894 MiB awake, 3 MiB napping. OpenCode in total, server included: 1,172 MiB awake, 294 MiB napping.](docs/memory.svg) OpenCode 2.2.4 on Linux, ten windows on the start screen, measured as proportional set size (PSS), which counts memory that processes share only once. Windows with long sessions use more while awake (134 MiB each across ten long real sessions) and the same 0.3 MiB napping, so everyday savings are larger. Measure your own with scripts/measure-memory.sh. Work keeps running while a window naps, because sessions live in the OpenCode server, not in the window. It works in any terminal, inside or outside tmux, with nothing else to install. **This plugin was not built by the OpenCode team and is not affiliated with them.** ## Install Add it to your global `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` or a project's `opencode.json`: ```json { "plugins": ["opencode-nap"] } ``` Restart your OpenCode windows. Each one naps after 15 minutes without input. ## Options Use the object form in the same file to set options: ```json { "plugins": [ { "package": "opencode-nap", "options": { "idleMinutes": 10, "napOnBlur": true } } ] } ``` | Option | Default | Meaning | | ----------------- | ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `idleMinutes` | `15` | Minutes without input before a window naps. Fractions are allowed. | | `napOnBlur` | `false` | Nap a couple of seconds after the terminal loses focus. | | `blurIdleMinutes` | unset | A shorter idle time that applies while the terminal is unfocused. | | `carryDraft` | `true` | Bring back unsent prompt text after a nap. | | `enabled` | `true` | Set to `false` to turn the plugin off without removing it. | | `debugLogFile` | unset | Absolute path of a diagnostic log. It never contains prompt text. | Input means a key press, a paste or mouse input. The focus options need a terminal that reports focus changes; without them, only `idleMinutes` applies. A window that napped while unfocused also wakes when you switch back to it; one that napped while focused waits for a key or click. An unknown or invalid option turns the plugin off. ## How it works When a window has been idle long enough, the OpenCode process replaces itself with a tiny shell script that waits. It first draws OpenCode's logo in your theme's colours, with the working directory and a short note that the window is napping. The screen is drawn once, so it stays as it was if you resize the terminal or change the theme while the window naps; a terminal too small for it gets a line of plain text. Press any key or click to wake it: OpenCode starts again in the same window and opens the same session. The key you pressed is not sent to OpenCode. Waking takes a second or two. A running session carries on in the server the whole time, and a permission or question prompt that comes up while the window naps is waiting for you when it wakes. A window on OpenCode's background service wakes straight into that service with `--server`, using the address and password OpenCode registers in `~/.local/state/opencode/service.json` (under `$XDG_STATE_HOME` if set). A plain start would check the service first and replace it if it is slow to answer, which ends every window's terminals and shells, and several windows waking together can keep it that slow. A busy service gets waited for instead, with a line saying so; Ctrl-C stops waiting and starts OpenCode the usual way. The waiting uses `curl`; without it the window connects at once, and if the service then takes more than five seconds to answer, OpenCode exits with an error instead of replacing the service. The window starts the usual way when nothing is registered, the registered process is gone, the service is a different version from the one the window napped from, or the service refuses the connection or the password. A window woken like this reconnects if the service restarts, since OpenCode keeps the same address and password, and reads the registration again at its next nap. A window you started with `--server` wakes with the same `--server` as before. After a wake you get the same session, prompt history, open tabs, selected model and any unsent prompt text. The view starts fresh, as it does after a normal restart: scroll position resets, and the agent and model variant go back to their defaults. Attachments and images in an unsent prompt are not kept. ## When it does not nap The plugin turns itself off for a window when napping could lose work or is not possible: - OpenCode runs with `--standalone`, so the session lives inside the window. - OpenCode was started with a subcommand or an option the plugin does not recognise. - The platform is not macOS or Linux, or the terminal is not a real terminal. - An OpenCode internal the plugin relies on has changed. It waits and tries again a few seconds later while an external editor has the terminal, or while unsent prompt text cannot be saved. ## Platforms macOS and Linux. On Windows the plugin does nothing. ## Development ```sh bun install npm run ci:check # lint, typecheck, unit tests npm run build npm run test:e2e # drives real OpenCode windows against a local fake model ``` The end-to-end runner builds and installs the packed package once, then runs up to eight isolated test processes. Long files are split into complementary groups, so every case still runs. Processes share only installed dependencies: each gets its own HOME, XDG directories, project, temporary files and private servers. Short idle settings exercise the real nap timers without waiting minutes. The tests never call a hosted model. ## License MIT. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).
